newsitem.title: GERMANY: German wise man argues for delaying monetary union.
newsitem.headline: German wise man argues for delaying monetary union.

text.p: A top German economist said on Friday a delay in the start of European monetary union could be the answer if Bonn missed the EMU entry criteria, but Chancellor Helmut Kohl immediately ruled out such a scenario.

Juergen Donges, one of the panel of economic advisers known as the five wise men, told Reuters in an interview he saw no chance for Germany to meet the EMU targets on either the budget deficit or public debt assessments.
He added he did not believe the stability pact on EMU (economic and monetary union) fully ensured that countries joining the single currency would keep their budgets under control.

But Kohl reaffirmed the official line on EMU to industrialists in Duesseldorf. "I stand by both the stability criteria in the Maastricht Treaty as well as the timetable," he said. "Germany will never accept a delay in the timetable."

Donges said that if EMU could not begin on schedule in 1999 with enough countries, then it would be better to delay the start. It was more important to ensure that the criteria were met adequately than to start on time, he said.
"History will measure monetary union on the criteria of whether it really produces a stable currency and not on the basis of whether it began on a certain day," he said.
Countries which wish to enter monetary union in 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, total debt and public deficits this year, as laid down in the 1993 Maastricht Treaty.

For most countries the deficit requirement, which calls for a deficit equal to no more than three percent of gross domestic product, is proving the hardest to meet. Germany is aiming for a 2.9 percent level this year, which many see as optimistic.
On public debt, the ideal target is 60 percent of GDP. Countries with much higher debt levels must at least show that they are making progress toward that level.

Germany is currently running a debt level of just over 60 percent which is set to rise this year, but has already pleaded that the special situation of German unification should warrant it special treatment in the final assessment.
The European Commission forecast on Wednesday that Germany would hit the Maastricht deficit target on the head, with a 3.0 percent deficit this year.
But Germany's six major economic insititutes were more sceptical, forecasting 3.0 to 3.2 percent.
The institutes said, however, that they believed monetary union should go ahead on time even if Germany overshot this one target by a relatively small margin.

Donges said he believed it was essential EMU should start with a large group of countries, rather than starting out as a community of two classes, particularly in the instance where even those inside EMU had not met the criteria.

"I have to ask why you can turn a blind eye in the case of those countries which were always intended to belong to the core group while countries such as Spain or Portugal, which have made enormous, convincing steps toward convergence, have to remain outside," he said.

Donges criticised the stability pact aimed at ensuring discipline within monetary union, saying the plan left too many loopholes open. "If a big country steps out of line then even a five (percent deficit ratio) might go unpunished," he said.

The stability pact, agreed in Dublin, Ireland in December and finalised in Noordwijk, Netherlands earlier this month sets sanctions and fines for countries which exceed a three percent budget deficit.
